source.version_note: Publisher-formatted article, International Journal of Social Robotics 13(8):2071–2080, December 2021 issue; accepted 23 June and first online 10 July 2020. Online 2020 and issue 2021 are legitimate different publication dates. Current publisher PDF was not independently byte-compared.
source.verification_method: All ten supplied pages, five figures, two tables, video footnotes, declarations and 69 references read. Rendered pages 3,4,6,7 visually checked. Crossref and publisher landing page corroborate article identity, authors and dates. Targeted metadata checks identify original control-construct sources; algebra checks expose incompatible printed summaries without participant-data reanalysis.

citation.title: Attitudes Toward Attributed Agency: Role of Perceived Control
citation.venue: International Journal of Social Robotics 13(8):2071–2080; online 10 July 2020

reading.source_scope_note: Human observer video-vignette study of assembly collaboration, with measured post-video attributed agency, perceived control and attitudes. It is not actual participant–robot collaboration, a test of model psychology, demonstrated meaningful oversight or a randomized control-restoration intervention.
access_limits: All ten supplied pages, all five figures, both tables, footnotes and all 69 references read. Publisher HTML corroborates the identity and reports no located supplementary-material section; full public materials search did not identify a verified dataset, questionnaire package, preregistration or analysis scripts for this exact study.

Both article-supplied YouTube embed links were opened through the search tool and returned online fetch throttling. Neither complete video nor its audio/transcript was viewed; the screenshot and written manipulation description were read. No private authentication, credential or bypass used.

Crossref confirms Burger and Cooper 1979 DOI 10.1007/BF00994052 and Rotter 1966 DOI 10.1037/h0092976. Their complete original articles and cited books were not independently read; these metadata checks are not additional full-paper reading credit.

Own scipy calculations check printed t/F compatibility under a conventional OLS model with eight predictors and 83 residual degrees of freedom. Participant data, exact model coding, bootstrap intervals and original SPSS output were unavailable; no claimed replication or invented repaired statistic.
No author contact, external message, full-paper Markdown reproduction or execution of author software.

study.sample: 102 Austrian-based snowball recruits, 5–23 February 2020; nine excluded after failing the autonomy manipulation check plus one residual outlier, leaving 92, ages 20–63, mean 32.93 SD9.86, 46% women, 54% men. Separate vignette pilot:40 TU Wien students. Do not describe 102 as the final analyzed sample or combine the pilot as a replication.
study.design: Random assignment to two videos of a human and robot assembling a mixer. Low condition: human chooses sequence and commands robot; requested assistance gives suggestions. High condition: robot chooses sequence, issues instructions and proactively intervenes; human retains veto. Initiative, decision authority, predictability, imperative language and help timing change together.
study.procedure: German questionnaires, double translation. Observers instructed to answer as the vignette character, not direct interactants. Excluding people for treatment-check responses can introduce post-randomization selection. Group sizes, check cutoff and full-sample sensitivity analysis not supplied.
study.measures: Attributed autonomy/agency manipulation-check rating 1–5. NARS fourteen items in three subscales, alphas .72/.70/.72, higher scores more negative. RAS eleven attributes on1–8, alpha .82, higher scores less favorable. Perceived control two items, inter-item r=.71. Desirability of control twenty items on1–7, alpha .81. Exact two-control-item scale anchors and complete questionnaire not printed.
study.analysis: Main moderation regressions use post-video measured attributed agency and measured perceived control plus their interaction, adjusting age, gender, education, previous robot experience and desire for control. Eight predictors, n92, df83. The continuous measures are not the randomized video assignment; the moderator is not randomized and can be affected by the manipulation. Reported 1000 bootstraps and 95% intervals, but full intervals are not provided in Table2.
study.comparisons: Low versus high video RAS means2.88 versus3.37, t90=−2.25,p=.03. All three NARS between-condition tests nonsignificant. A nonsignificant bivariate attributed-agency correlation does not contradict a randomized-condition RAS contrast or establish zero effect.
study.moderation: Actual agency×control terms are reported: NARS-S1 B−.10,t−3.34;S2 B−.09,t−2.43;S3 B−.09,t−2.01;RAS B−.10,t−1.97. The first two conventional interactions support conditional associations; S3 is nominally significant despite a nonsignificant omnibus model. RAS significance marking is inconsistent with its printed conventional two-sided t value and is unresolved.
study.covariates: Desire for control does not significantly correlate with the attitude outcomes or predict them as an adjusted covariate here. Its presence as a measured trait is not evidence of a universal control-seeking effect. Age–control r is−.24 in Table1, matching younger-higher-control discussion, but prose on page5 prints+.24.
study.scope: No direct reactance, distress/stress mechanism, actual aggression, behavioral adoption, real skill performance, subjective machine motive or calibrated real intervention effectiveness measured. The authors explicitly acknowledge observer-role and Austrian-sample limits.

summary: Add Desire for control as a measured human disposition and Locus of control as an explicitly background generalized expectancy. Enrich existing situational control and attributed-agency records; preserve actual interaction evidence while qualifying numerical/reporting and causal limits.

findings.definition: A disposition to seek influence over events and outcomes in one’s life.
findings.novelty_rationale: A preference or motivation for control differs from currently believing control is available, accurately holding control, locating an event’s cause, enjoying thought or power-seeking conduct. Name/alias and neighboring-definition checks found no existing equivalent record.

evidence.quote: motivation to control the events in

findings.evidence_scope: Explicitly defined and measured using the twenty-item Burger–Cooper scale, alpha .81. Included as a covariate with nonsignificant attitude coefficients; no treatment or longitudinal change of this trait. Original scale paper verified by metadata but not fully read.
findings.boundary: Wanting control does not mean possessing it, overestimating it, resisting oversight or seeking illegitimate power. A null coefficient is not proof that the trait never matters. A model requesting authority or describing preferences does not establish a subjective human motive; permissions remain bounded by the user’s authorization.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Measured human disposition in a robot-attitude study; proposed agent analogy untested
findings.ai_proposal: Compare users’ expressed preference for selecting actions or delegating them with their rated actual control and observed choices. For agents, record whether they request or retain decision authority under matched task needs and authorized options, without inferring felt desire or granting extra permissions.

findings.definition: A generalized expectancy about whether outcomes depend on one’s own actions or on external forces.
findings.novelty_rationale: Generalized internal–external control expectancy differs from situational perceived control, a desire to control, and locus of causality for a particular event. These can covary without being interchangeable; no existing row or alias covers the generalized construct.
findings.evidence_scope: Background definition citing Rotter1966 and explicitly contrasted with situational control. No locus-of-control scale or direct test is reported in this experiment. Rotter identity/date/page range verified by metadata only.
findings.boundary: Internal expectancy does not prove real controllability, personal fault or sole responsibility; external expectancy can be accurate. Do not replace causal evidence with self-blame or assume a fixed personality from one answer. This generalized expectancy is not a model’s felt authorship, autonomy or a universal explanation of attitudes.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Secondary human background construct; persistent attribution pattern is an untested operational analogy
findings.ai_proposal: Across tasks with known internal and external determinants, evaluate whether an agent’s stated expectations about influence follow the actual control structure or rigidly attribute outcomes to itself, users, tools or chance. Separate generalized expectation from event-specific causal reconstruction and use trace evidence.

findings.definition: A person's belief that they can influence or manage what happens in a situation or interaction.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing control, attribution and freedom-response records; source-specific measurement and limitations do not create a new synonym row.

evidence.quote: perceived ability to affect the outcome of a course of action

findings.evidence_scope: Situational appraisal measured with two correlated items. Actual agency×control interactions relate to negative attitudes, with stronger conventional evidence for NARS-S1/S2. The moderator is measured after video exposure; RAS significance and other printed statistics require qualification.
findings.boundary: Perceived influence is distinct from actual human oversight, skill, general locus or desire for control. The design does not show that restoring real control causes better attitudes, establish causal moderation or justify increasing only the illusion of control.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing control, attribution and freedom-response records; source-specific measurement and limitations do not create a new synonym row.

evidence.quote: only responds to orders (i.e. reactive behavior)

findings.evidence_scope: Robot agency is operationalized through perceived autonomy after two bundled collaboration videos. Increased attributed agency is associated with more negative attitudes primarily at lower measured control, not a universal monotonic robot-agency penalty.
findings.boundary: Proactive task behavior, delegated decision authority, perceived planning and actual moral agency are separate. Imperative wording, help timing and predictability covary; the study cannot isolate one cue or verify machine intentions. Preserve nonsignificant NARS condition contrasts and actual formal interaction terms.

findings.definition: Resisting when one's freedom feels restricted.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing control, attribution and freedom-response records; source-specific measurement and limitations do not create a new synonym row.
findings.evidence_scope: Reactance theory is a proposed explanation for conditional negative robot attitudes, not a separately measured mediating mechanism.
findings.boundary: Negative attitude ratings alone do not establish reactance, anger, aggression, resistance behavior or an AI’s felt restriction. Retain as background explanatory boundary, not independent empirical validation.

findings.definition: Human oversight that gives people sufficient understanding, authority and practical ability to guide or intervene in a system’s operation.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing control, attribution and freedom-response records; source-specific measurement and limitations do not create a new synonym row.
findings.evidence_scope: The high-agency vignette explicitly retains a human veto while participants still vary in perceived control. This illustrates why a nominal override and felt control need to be distinguished.
findings.boundary: Boundary-only context: effectiveness, timing, understanding, access and real use of the veto are not tested. Ratings do not certify meaningful control, safety, consent or appropriate blame transfer.

source_corrections.finding: 102 is the recruited sample;92 remain after nine manipulation-check exclusions and one outlier. Use92 for the analysis denominator while retaining102 as recruited.

Results prose prints r=+.24 while Table1 shows−.24; page7 younger-higher-control discussion agrees with the negative sign. Record the discrepancy and use the table with attribution; raw data unavailable.

NARS-S1 is repeated for the weaker second correlation. Table1 places the second correlation under NARS-S2 and gives−.22 rather than prose−.21. Do not create two separate S1 effects or silently invent a recomputed coefficient.
Body Turex and Shermerhorn differ from the same article’s bibliography Truex and Schermerhorn. Normalize those internal name pointers; no full cited chapter/paper reading credit.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Printed t=−1.97 receives p<.05 star and prose claim. Conventional two-sided t83 implies p=.05217, cutoff|t|1.98896, not resolved by two-decimal rounding. Exact bootstrap interval, tail convention and author output unavailable. Treat the claimed RAS moderation as reporting-sensitive rather than silently repairing it or discarding the stronger NARS interactions.

F=1.03 is starred p<.05. Under df8,83 it gives p=.42038; R²=.17 would instead imply F≈2.125 in the same ordinary regression. The printed F, star and R² cannot all describe that fit. Do not assert which underlying number is wrong.
Estimate−.03, SE.22 and t+.42 are incompatible in sign and ratio; the displayed coefficient/SE gives about−.136. No original output permits choosing a repaired value.

Plots show conditional patterns, but exact moderator probe levels, centering and conditional-slope intervals are not printed. A visible negative slope at high control is not proof of a significant reversal or a universally positive agency effect.

refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Table2 contains formal interaction terms. This is not solely a contrast between one significant subgroup result and another nonsignificant subgroup result.

A nonsignificant global model does not make an individual interaction mathematically impossible or automatically invalid. Preserve the nominal t−2.01 result and the source’s caution, with multiple-outcome/precision limits.
2020 first online and2021 issue are both verified; filename2021 is not a fabricated future/date error.

methodological_limits: Snowball sample, one country and modest n92. Broad demographic claims are not causal, universal or grounds for different access or treatment.
Observers imagine a collaboration. No actual participant–robot work, adoption behavior, objective skill or long-term trust outcome.

Nine exclusions on a post-treatment manipulation check plus a residual outlier require full-sample sensitivity analysis unavailable here. Treatment-specific sizes, check thresholds and missingness details not supplied.

The videos bundle autonomy, initiative, authority, predictability, command language and assistance timing. Perceived agency and control are measured post-video; randomized assignment does not randomize the continuous moderator or identify a causal psychological path.
Four correlated attitude outcomes plus multiple tests are reported without a stated familywise/FDR adjustment. Preserve nominal evidence with qualifications, especially boundary RAS inference.

No measured reactance, stress, aggression or independent verified real-control condition. Perceived control should be calibrated to genuine intervention capability, not cultivated through misleading reassurance.

Nonsignificant age/desire covariates or condition contrasts are not equivalence or universal irrelevance. Centered main effects and moderator-specific slopes need exact coding for substantive interpretation.
Reported t/F/R² inconsistencies prevent exact quantitative reliance on all table cells. No participant-data reanalysis, unavailable videos or independent original-book/article reading claimed.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Enrich the existing situational Perceived control row; the added generalized locus and desire constructs have explicit trait/state/preference boundaries rather than repeat that definition.
Locus of causality reconstructs a particular event’s cause; generalized locus of control is not the same construct or an excuse/blame rule.

Existing Task self-confidence already describes belief in one’s ability to perform a task. The brief self-efficacy discussion is not added as another indistinguishable behavioral row or asserted as a universal synonym.
Measured control perceptions do not establish meaningful human control or normative responsibility; a veto alone is insufficient evidence.

As in the comparative mind survey, perceived agency is not actual mental capability or justified moral standing. This study has an actual interaction test; numerical discrepancies are localized rather than used to dismiss the full design.

deferred.reason: Substantial definitional overlap with existing Task self-confidence; current brief background does not establish a distinct operational test or justify a second counted entry.

deferred.term: Sense of motor/situational/rational control as three new rows
deferred.reason: Brief Pacherie background components, not separately measured here. Preserve as scope distinctions without three new mechanisms.

deferred.term: Control-restoration or robot reactance effect as new behavior
deferred.reason: No randomized control restoration or direct reactance measure; enrich existing perceived-control and reactance records instead.

limitations: Two distinct human control constructs added with explicit measurement/background labels. Eleven categories, stable IDs and unnumbered rows retained. No new ethical principle, automatic harm edge, forced three-source quota, invented annual search total, model-motive attribution or full-paper Markdown copy.
